newsitem.title: CANADA: Avenor lowers its merger offer for Repap.
newsitem.headline: Avenor lowers its merger offer for Repap.

text.p: Avenor Inc. on Monday lowered its all-stock offer for financially troubled Repap Enterprises Inc. after Avenor shareholders complained the original C$3.3 billion ($2.4 billion) bid was too high.
The two Montreal-based pulp and paper companies said their boards agreed to the amended offer, under which Avenor is offering one newly issued share of Avenor for every eight shares of Repap.
Analysts said the revised offer came in at about C$2.6 billion ($1.9 billion), $700 million ($518 million) lower than the original offer.
They said that more information was needed on the new offer before they could determine whether the merger was in the best interests of Avenor shareholders.
Avenor's original bid, made Dec. 18, offered one Avenor share for every 4.25 shares of Repap. Under the original offer, Avenor also planned to assume Repap's C$2.4 billion ($1.78 billion) of debt.
But Repap's operations in the west coast province of British Columbia, which carried C$480 million ($355 million) of debt, will be exluded from the revised offer.
Analysts said Avenor had little choice but to lower the offer after shareholders indicated their disapproval of the original offer by hammering Repap's stock price.
Repap's stock slipped to C$2.42 on the Toronto Stock Exchange in the weeks after the December offer, from about C$5 at the time of the bid.
After the revised offer was announced on Monday, Repap shares rose C33 cents to C$2.75 in Toronto and by 16 cents to $1.94 on Nasdaq.
Avenor shares were off C55 cents to C$23.25 in Toronto.

"The amended agreement benefits all shareholders of the new Avenor," Avenor Chief Executive Paul Gagne said in a statement. "The removal of Repap B.C. from the transaction contributes to reduce both the debt level and the share dilution caused by the transaction," he said.

Avenor said that under the revised offer, it would not proceed with the originally planned private placements of C$75 million ($55.5 million) of common shares and C$140 million ($104 million) of convertible debentures. That would reduce the dilution of Avenor shares, it said.
"We're all sitting on the fence waiting for more details," said John Duncanson, an independent analyst based in Toronto.

One key concern that remains is the roughly C$2.7 billion ($2 billion) of debt the merged company would have on its books. Avenor said it planned to proceed with the divestiture of its operations in British Columbia and the Repap pulp mill in Manitoba for gross proceeds of C$500 million ($370 million).
Avenor shareholders will vote on the new offer on March 26.
